newsitem.title: USA: Wheat prices at their lowest since August 1994.
newsitem.headline: Wheat prices at their lowest since August 1994.

text.p: Wheat prices slumped on Monday to the lowest level since August 1994 as this year's harvest progressed rapidly amid hot, dry weather in the U.S. Plains.
"Yields are much better than expected and quality is much better than expected in the hard red and soft red areas," said Charlie Sernatinger, an analyst for E.D. and F. Man International.
Dealers said conditions for the U.S. wheat crop have been almost ideal for the last couple of months, allowing it to recover from a late freeze.

At the Chicago Board of Trade, prices for soft red winter wheat for delivery in July have dipped from a high of $4.59 a bushel in April to a low on Monday of $3.28, the cheapest level for the nearby contract in almost three years. July wheat closed five cents lower at $3.29-3/4.
The U.S. Department of Agriculture reported Monday that 67 percent of the U.S. winter wheat crop was in good or excellent condition as of Sunday, up from 33 percent a year ago.
Wheat harvesting was under way in many states, including Kansas and Oklahoma, both key areas for hard red winter wheat, and Arkansas, an important soft red winter wheat region.
One trader based in Kansas City said he was hearing yield estimates for Kansas in the range of 40 to 60 bushels per acre. In 1996, Kansas wheat yields averaged 34 bushels.
Corn prices were also lower as this year's crop continued to flourish in the U.S. Midwest amid favorable weather.
"I can't imagine a situation where we could get much better weather than this present scenario," Sernatinger said.
Weakness in wheat prices also hurt corn values.
"The fact we're getting such huge yields in wheat cuts into feed needs for corn," Sernatinger said.
CBOT corn for July delivery closed five cents a bushel lower at $2.60-1/2.
At the New York Mercantile Exchange, crude oil prices ended higher amid increasing tensions between the United Nations and Iraq and statements by Iran bemoaning the decline in oil prices.

"When you have talk of the U.N. Security Council taking action against Iraq because it denied weapons inspectors access, it's bound to lead to short-covering (buying)," said Warren Tashnek, president of Fimat USA Futures in Houston.

August crude ended up 25 cents at $19.14 a barrel. Refined products followed crude higher, dealers said. July gasoline ended 0.16 cent higher at 55.64 cents a gallon while July heating oil finished up 0.59 cent at 51.92 cents a gallon.

Crude started the session strong after the Security Council adopted a resolution over the weekend threatening Iraq with further sanctions if it does not allow U.N. arms inspectors to search sensitive sites.

On June 10 and 12, U.N. inspectors were prevented from searching three sites for weapons of mass destruction and related materials. Although the Security Council threatened additional measures against Iraq, it would need to adopt another resolution to impose them.

A deal easing current U.N. sanctions against Iraq remains in place. That agreement allows Iraq to sell $2 billion worth of oil every six months on a renewable basis in exchange for food and humanitarian aid.
There was no linkage between the oil-for-food deal and the current U.N.-Iraq tensions, but dealers were concerned there could be if tensions escalate.

Iranian oil minister Gholamreza Aghazadeh said on Monday he was not satisfied with oil prices and said OPEC should take steps to stop quota violations. Aghazadeh made his statement in Vienna ahead of a summer ministerial meeting of the Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries which officially starts there on Wednesday.

Still, traders expect OPEC ministers to extend the group's self-imposed production ceiling of 25.03 million barrels per day even though widespread quota-busting has boosted OPEC output by 2 million barrels above that level.
